summary: TRILL routes frames through multi-hop networks with arbitrary topologies. This document extends its labeling of data packets beyond the base protocol's limit, so more separate groups of traffic can be told apart.

plainLanguage.summary: TRILL's fine-grained labeling extension gives packets a larger label space than VLAN labeling. Switches use the label to keep traffic separated and to decide where packets may leave the network.

questions: how many labels does trill fgl support
subtitle: TRILL adds 24-bit labels for traffic that needs fine-grained isolation.

tldr.problem: Base TRILL labels data with a VLAN-sized set of IDs, which is too small for networks that need configurable isolation among many users.
tldr.mechanism: Fine-grained labeling adds a 24-bit label in TRILL data packets and defines rules to keep FGL packets away from switches that cannot safely process them.
tldr.outcome: FGL is an optional extension to TRILL that provides 2^24 labels. RFC 7172 updates RFC 6325.

today: RFC 7172 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2014. It updates the TRILL base specification, RFC 6325.

sections.title: Why TRILL Needs More Labels
sections.content:
TRILL routes frames through multi-hop networks using link-state routing and a hop count. The base protocol supports up to 4K data labels, while some networks need more labels to isolate tenants, services, or other groups.

RFC 7172 defines optional fine-grained labeling (FGL), intended in particular for large data centers with more than 4K users who need configurable separation.
sections.plainLanguage: The base TRILL label space can be too small for networks with many isolated groups. FGL adds a much larger set of labels for those networks.

sections.title: The Fine-Grained Label Format
sections.content:
An FGL is a 24-bit label divided into a 12-bit high part and a 12-bit low part. After the inner MAC addresses, an FGL packet carries Ethertype 0x893B, the high part, the same Ethertype again, and the low part.

Each 16-bit part also contains a 3-bit priority and a Drop Eligibility Indicator bit. The high-part priority is used across the TRILL campus; the low-part priority is retained from the original frame and restored on egress.
sections.plainLanguage: The label has a high and low part, and together they identify the traffic group. Each part also carries priority information for forwarding and delivery.

sections.title: Ingress, Transit, and Egress
sections.content:
An ingress switch maps a native frame's C-VLAN to an FGL label, using a configurable per-port mapping. Transit switches forward FGL traffic and use the high-part priority. For multi-destination traffic, they may prune branches that have no interest in the label.

At egress, a switch maps the FGL back to a C-VLAN and restores priority from the low part. A switch MUST NOT send an FGL packet out a port that is not configured for that FGL, even if the VLAN number matches part of the label.
sections.plainLanguage: The ingress switch maps a frame to an FGL label. Transit switches forward it, and the egress switch maps it back only on a port configured for that label.

sections.title: Coexisting with VLAN-Only Switches
sections.content:
A VLAN-labeled (VL) switch that is not FGL-safe may misread an FGL packet, send it into the wrong VLAN, or prune a distribution tree incorrectly. FGL-safe switches advertise their capability so the network can identify devices that cannot safely handle FGL.

When FGL is in use, an adjacent FGL-safe switch must block FGL packets from a VL neighbor or assign the adjacency a cost that removes it from normal path selection. FGL distribution trees must be rooted at an FGL-safe switch or FGL link pseudonode.
sections.plainLanguage: Older switches may not understand FGL packets. The network marks safe switches and routes FGL traffic so it does not pass through a switch that may mishandle it.

sections.title: IS-IS and Label Registrations
sections.content:
TRILL switches announce FGL-safe capability and FGL label interest through IS-IS extensions. Related sub-TLVs describe interested labels and group addresses for FGL.

The IEEE Registration Authority assigned Ethertype 0x893B to TRILL FGL. IANA allocated capability flag 1 in the TRILL-VER sub-TLV to indicate that a switch is FGL-safe.
sections.plainLanguage: TRILL switches exchange information about their FGL capability and the labels they use. Assigned values let other switches recognize FGL packets and capabilities.

sections.title: Preventing Label Confusion
sections.content:
A switch that confuses a VLAN label with an FGL label could send data to the wrong VLAN or incorrectly prune a multi-destination packet. All TRILL switches MUST check the Ethertype after the inner source MAC address.

If a switch does not recognize that Ethertype, it must discard the frame or make no forwarding decisions based on fields after it. FGL traffic must also be kept away from VL switches that are not FGL-safe.
sections.plainLanguage: Switches must check which kind of label a packet carries before forwarding it. This prevents traffic from crossing into a group that should remain separate.
